original_question: Let the consecutive sequence in base 10 begin 1, 12, 123, 1234, and continue by concatenating consecutive positive integers. Determine how many primes occur in that sequence, and more generally solve the same prime-counting problem for the analogous sequence in an arbitrary numeration base B.
target_in_paper: Section 2.2, "Consecutive sequence [16]": the open problem asking, for the displayed decimal concatenation sequence, "How many primes are there among these numbers?" and then extending the same question to an arbitrary numeration base B.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core content of the paper-faithfully: it identifies the same decimal sequence beginning 1, 12, 123, 1234, formed by concatenating consecutive positive integers; it asks the same prime-counting question for that sequence; and it includes the paper's explicit generalization to an arbitrary numeration base B.
missing_details: The paper gives this as the "Consecutive Sequence"; naming it helps match the source exactly.
The arbitrary base should be quantified explicitly as an integer base B >= 2.

For each n >= 1, the nth term should be defined precisely as the integer whose base-B expansion is the concatenation of the standard base-B representations of 1, 2, ..., n, written without leading zeros.
It should be made explicit that primality is taken in the ordinary integers Z, after interpreting the concatenated base-B numeral as an integer.
The generalization should be phrased as: for each fixed base B >= 2, determine how many prime terms occur in the corresponding base-B consecutive sequence.
No further hypotheses, asymptotic qualifiers, or auxiliary conditions appear in the paper; the source statement is a bare open problem in a problem list.
refined_question: For each integer base B >= 2, let [m]_B denote the standard base-B expansion of the positive integer m, written without leading zeros, and define C_B(n) to be the positive integer whose base-B expansion is the concatenation [1]_B[2]_B...[n]_B. Thus, in base 10, C_10(1)=1, C_10(2)=12, C_10(3)=123, C_10(4)=1234, and so on. Determine how many terms of the Consecutive Sequence {C_10(n)}_{n>=1} are prime; more generally, for each fixed base B >= 2, determine how many terms of {C_B(n)}_{n>=1} are prime.
justification: Section 2.2 states exactly this problem in two sentences: it first displays the decimal consecutive concatenation sequence and asks how many primes occur among its terms, then immediately says that, in general form, the Consecutive Sequence is considered in an arbitrary numeration base B. The draft is therefore already very close to the paper. To make it fully stand-alone and paper-faithful, the only real additions are the exact base-B term definition, the quantifier B >= 2, and the clarification that primality is in Z for the integer represented by the concatenated base-B numeral. The problem is posed as an open problem in the paper's mathematics problem list, and the paper does not provide a proved equivalent reformulation nearby.
